scenes.title: Passing Secret Values
scenes.narration: Lab 17 masked the admin password with one flag and moved on. This lesson gives secrets their full treatment: the three ways to pass a sensitive value, what masking really does, and the one place your secret still ends up in plain text.

scenes.heading: Three paths to a secret
points: terraform.tfvars — auto-loaded, but must be gitignored for secrets
TF_VAR_<name> environment variable — per-shell, never touches disk
-var on the command line — convenient, but lands in shell history
sensitive = true masks logs; the state file remains plain text
scenes.narration: Terraform gives you three doors for a secret, and each has a price. The t f vars file is convenient and auto-loaded — but it's a file, so it belongs in git ignore, never in the repository. The T F V A R environment variable keeps the secret off disk entirely, but only for that shell session. The var flag is quick for tests — and it lands in your shell history, so think twice. And whatever path you choose, the sensitive flag only masks the logs. The state file keeps the value in plain text — protect it accordingly.

scenes.narration: As always, the lab is in the course GitHub repository under Section 1, Foundations, with the link in the description. Note the file list: a terraform dot t f vars dot example, not a real one — the real t f vars is gitignored, by design.

The two variables. Admin username — not secret, just a default of azureadmin. And admin password: type string, sensitive true, no default. Terraform will mask this value in every log, and prompt for it if nothing supplies one. The declaration alone already changes what appears on screen.

The machine, and the two lines that matter: admin username and admin password, both flowing from the variables. The password reaches the V M exactly like any other attribute — but because the variable is sensitive, it never prints in plain text in the plan or the apply.

This is the example file — one line, an obviously fake password. Its whole job is documentation: it shows the shape a real t f vars file needs. The real file, terraform dot t f vars, holds the actual password and lives in git ignore, where no push can ever reach it.

scenes.caption: Three paths, one masked destination
scenes.narration: The three delivery paths drawn out: a gitignored t f vars file, the T F V A R environment variable, and the command line var — all feeding the same sensitive variable, which masks the value in every log before it reaches the machine.

steps.narration: Path one: a t f vars file — auto-loaded, and gitignored, because it holds the real value.
Path two: the T F V A R environment variable — set per shell, never written to disk.
Path three: the var flag on the command line — quick, but it lands in shell history.
All three feed the same sensitive variable — masked in every plan and apply log.
And the value flows into the machine — usable, but never printed. Only the state file still holds it in plain text.

scenes.narration: Apply time — five resources, and one detail that proves the flag worked: nowhere in that log does the password appear. The variable was sensitive, so Terraform printed a placeholder instead. The machine got the real value; the terminal got nothing. That's masking working exactly as intended.

scenes.heading: Common pitfall — trusting the mask with the secret itself
points: sensitive masks logs — the value still sits in state, in plain text
Never commit a real tfvars — ship the .example, gitignore the real file
-var leaks into shell history; TF_VAR_ stays per-shell
Rotate any secret that ever reached a log, a file, or a history
scenes.narration: Here are the pitfalls in this lab. One: sensitive masks logs — the value still sits in state, in plain text. The mask protects the log, nothing more; protect the state file like the secret it holds. Two: never commit a real t f vars file — ship the example, and gitignore the real one. The file that carries the real value stays local; the committed template documents its shape. Three: a var flag leaks into shell history; a t f underscore v a r environment variable stays per-shell. What you type on the command line is recorded; environment variables are not. Four: rotate any secret that ever reached a log, a file, or a history. If a secret leaked, the fix isn't masking — it's rotation.

points: sensitive = masked in plan/apply logs — not encryption
Three paths for a secret: gitignored tfvars, TF_VAR_ env var, -var flag
tfvars.example documents the shape; the real file never gets committed
The state file still holds the value in plain text — protect it
A secret that reached a log, file, or history is a rotated secret
scenes.narration: Quick recap — five things. One: sensitive means masked in plan and apply logs — not encryption. Two: three paths for a secret — a gitignored t f vars file, a t f underscore v a r environment variable, or a var flag. Three: the t f vars example documents the shape; the real file never gets committed. Four: the state file still holds the value in plain text — protect it. Five: a secret that reached a log, a file, or a history is a rotated secret.
Now that we understand how this Terraform configuration works, in the next part of this video, we'll move to a real-world demo and deploy it in Microsoft Azure.
